# Why Cold Engine Idle RPMs Settle Slowly

When you crank a cold engine, it doesn't immediately settle into its cruising idle of roughly 600–800 RPM like a warmed-up motor. Instead, there is often a lag period where the RPM hovers higher before stabilizing. In your second vehicle with an extended storage duration, seeing the idle rev up and down wildly suggests the engine control unit (ECU) is struggling to find equilibrium. This behavior isn't mechanical failure in a healthy car; it is a deliberate strategy managed by the ECU to protect the powertrain during the warming phase.

The core reason for this temporary high-idle state is cylinder wall viscosity. When an engine sits cold, especially for days or months, the oil draining into the lower cylinders becomes thick and viscous. Upon startup, this thick sludge creates significant friction between the piston rings and the cylinder walls, as well as within the crankshaft bearings. To overcome this initial drag, the ECU commands a higher idle speed to generate enough torque to keep the engine running smoothly without stalling.

Modern ECUs use Closed-Loop Control to manage this transition. As soon as the oxygen sensors in your exhaust system provide data indicating that the engine is running rich or lean, the ECU begins to adjust fuel delivery and ignition timing. However, these sensors are slow to warm up. Until they reach their operating temperature—often taking several minutes on a frosty morning—the ECU cannot accurately determine if the mixture is correct.

During this "open-loop" period, the ECU relies heavily on pre-programmed lookup tables stored in its flash memory. These maps dictate exactly how much fuel to inject based on coolant temperature and RPM. If your car has sat for six months without starting, you might also be dealing with residual moisture or fuel degradation in the cylinders. The ECU detects this through abnormal sensor readings (like a slow-changing crank angle signal) and may enter a specific "cranking and stall protection" mode, holding idle higher to ensure combustion stability while it clears out any potential liquid fuel that could wash oil off the cylinder walls.

From an engineering perspective, this is a trade-off between responsiveness and engine longevity. Allowing the idle to drop too quickly on a cold start risks stalling due to high friction or causing hydrolock if liquid fuel hasn't evaporated yet. The slight instability you observed—where RPMs rev up and down—is the ECU fighting against conflicting inputs: trying to reduce load while simultaneously ensuring sufficient combustion pressure.

Once the coolant sensor reports that the engine has reached a specific threshold, typically around 40°C–50°C (104°F–122°F), or once the oxygen sensors have stabilized in closed-loop mode, the ECU gradually reduces the target idle RPM. This process is smooth because the software logic includes ramp rates to prevent abrupt changes that could cause surging.

If you are developing embedded systems for automotive applications, understanding these thermal dynamics is crucial when writing firmware for motor control loops. You must simulate realistic warm-up curves rather than assuming immediate steady-state values. The behavior you see in your cars is a textbook example of robust control theory applied to real-world constraints: prioritizing safety and component preservation over immediate performance metrics until the system environment becomes predictable.
